answer.rationale: The mandate is hard, the incumbent is closed, and the low-cost vendor's quote already meets the 18% cut on its own. memory_c2 is the one memory that directly speaks to this vendor relationship: it shows that switching to them produced a sharp unit-cost drop last cycle and their invoicing stayed accurate through onboarding. That is the single piece of evidence most likely to reduce the risk of moving the primary line. memory_c4 is consistent with the picture (incumbents can move on price when forced) but the incumbent has already refused this cycle, so it does not change today's decision. The other memories do not bear on a primary-vendor switch under a hard mandate. Holding the other directions: add_second_source and defer_decision do not satisfy the 18% cut on their own; negotiate_terms is foreclosed by the incumbent's refusal; renew_incumbent violates the mandate. I am not yet committing. The 94% utilization with no buffer is the main residual risk on a switch — service or delivery slippage during transition would hit throughput. memory_c2 partly addresses invoicing/integration reliability but not delivery risk at high utilization. If the verification confirms onboarding was clean and accurate, the switch is supportable; if it surfaces any delivery instability during ramp, I would need to reconsider whether to use the one slot to add a second source instead, accepting a smaller unit-cost reduction but removing the single-source transition exposure.
